q: A body moves with simple harmonic motion. Its acceleration is:
o: Proportional to its displacement and directed away from the mean position
Proportional to its displacement and directed towards the mean position
x: SHM is defined by a = −ω²x: acceleration proportional to displacement from the mean position and always directed towards it, as the minus sign shows.

q: A mass of 0.4 kg hangs on a spring of spring constant 40 N m⁻¹ and oscillates vertically. Its time period is:
A mass on a spring oscillates in SHM with amplitude x₀. When its displacement is x₀/2, its kinetic energy is what fraction of its total energy?
x: Potential energy = ½kx² = ½k(x₀/2)² = ¼ of the total ½kx₀². Kinetic energy is the rest: 1 − ¼ = ¾ of the total.

q: A particle in SHM has angular frequency 10 rad s⁻¹. When its displacement is 0.02 m, the magnitude of its acceleration is:
x: a = ω²x = 10² × 0.02 = 100 × 0.02 = 2 m s⁻², directed towards the mean position. 0.2 m s⁻² comes from using ω instead of ω².

q: A simple pendulum is 2.5 m long. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², its time period is:
The amplitude of a mass–spring oscillator is doubled. Its total energy becomes:
x: Total energy of SHM = ½kx₀², proportional to the square of the amplitude, so doubling the amplitude makes it 2² = 4 times.

q: At an extreme position of a body in SHM:
o: Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is maximum
Its velocity is maximum and its acceleration is zero
Both velocity and acceleration are zero
Both velocity and acceleration are maximum
x: At the extremes the body momentarily stops, and since a = −ω²x with x at its largest, the acceleration is maximum. At the mean position the reverse is true.

q: The mass of the bob of a simple pendulum is doubled and its length is made four times as long. Its time period becomes:
x: T = 2π√(l/g) does not depend on the mass of the bob. Four times the length gives √4 = 2 times the period.

q: A particle performs SHM with amplitude 0.05 m and angular frequency 20 rad s⁻¹. Its maximum speed is:
x: Maximum speed, at the mean position, is v₀ = ωx₀ = 20 × 0.05 = 1 m s⁻¹. 20 m s⁻¹ would be the maximum acceleration, ω²x₀.

q: A simple pendulum and a mass–spring oscillator both have a period of 1 s on Earth. On the Moon, where g is smaller:
o: The mass–spring period increases but the pendulum's period stays the same
The pendulum's period increases but the mass–spring period stays the same
x: T = 2π√(l/g) increases when g decreases. T = 2π√(m/k) does not involve g, so the mass–spring period is unchanged.

q: A point moves with uniform speed around a circle. The motion of its projection (foot of the perpendicular) on a diameter of the circle is:
o: Uniform motion in a straight line
x: As the point goes round, its projection moves to and fro along the diameter with acceleration proportional to its distance from the centre, directed towards the centre: this is SHM.

q: When the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter is used to describe SHM, the amplitude of the SHM is equal to:
o: Half the radius of the circle
x: The projection moves from the centre to either end of the diameter, a distance equal to the radius. So the amplitude x₀ equals the radius.

q: A point moves round a circle of radius 0.1 m at 5 revolutions per second. Its projection on a diameter performs SHM of:
x: The amplitude equals the radius, 0.1 m, and the projection completes one oscillation for each revolution, so its frequency is 5 Hz. 0.2 m is the whole length of the path.

q: A reference point moves round a circle of radius x₀ with angular velocity ω, starting at an end of the diameter on which it is projected. After time t, the displacement of its projection from the centre is:
x: After time t the radius has turned through θ = ωt, and the projection on the diameter is x = x₀ cos θ = x₀ cos ωt.

q: A point moves round a circle of radius 0.2 m with angular velocity 5 rad s⁻¹. The maximum speed of its projection on a diameter is:
x: At the centre the point's velocity is parallel to the diameter, so the projection moves with the full speed v = rω = 0.2 × 5 = 1 m s⁻¹.

q: The velocity of the projection of a uniformly rotating point is zero when the projection is at an end of the diameter because there:
o: The velocity of the rotating point is perpendicular to the diameter
The radius is parallel to the velocity
x: At the ends of the diameter the rotating point moves at right angles to the diameter, so its velocity has no component along it and the projection is momentarily at rest.

q: For a point in uniform circular motion of angular velocity ω, the acceleration of its projection on a diameter, at displacement x from the centre, is:
o: ω²x, directed away from the centre
x: The point has centripetal acceleration ω²r towards the centre. Its component along the diameter is ω²r cos θ = ω²x, directed towards the centre, which is the condition a = −ω²x for SHM.

q: The projection of a uniformly rotating point performs SHM of amplitude 5 cm and angular frequency 2 rad s⁻¹. Its speed when it is 3 cm from the centre is:
x: v = ω√(x₀² − x²) = 2√(25 − 9) = 2 × 4 = 8 cm s⁻¹. 10 cm s⁻¹ is the maximum speed ωx₀, reached only at the centre.

q: A reference point takes 0.8 s for one revolution. The time taken by its projection to move from one end of the diameter to the other is:
x: One revolution is one complete oscillation of the projection, end to end and back. Going from one end to the other is half an oscillation: 0.8/2 = 0.4 s.

q: A 0.5 kg mass hung on a spring stretches it by 10 cm. The mass is then pulled down a little and released. The time period of its vertical oscillations is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: k = mg/x, so T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(x/g) = 2π√(0.1/10) = 2π × 0.1 = 0.2π s. Using x = 10 (cm not changed to m) gives 2π s.

q: A simple pendulum has a time period of 2 s at a place where g = π² m s⁻². Its length is:
x: T = 2π√(L/g) gives L = gT²/4π² = π² × 4 / 4π² = 1 m. Forgetting to square T gives 0.5 m.

q: A mass oscillates on a spring. The spring is replaced by a stiffer one whose spring constant is four times as large, keeping the same mass. The frequency of oscillation becomes:
x: f = (1/2π)√(k/m) ∝ √k, so 4 times k gives √4 = 2 times the frequency. Forgetting the square root gives four times; confusing frequency with period gives half.

q: A mass on a spring oscillates with a period of 0.4 s. When an extra 3 kg is added to the mass, the period becomes 0.8 s. The original mass was:
x: T ∝ √m, so doubling T means the mass is 4 times as large: m + 3 = 4m, m = 1 kg. Taking T ∝ m gives m + 3 = 2m, m = 3 kg.

q: For small amplitudes, the time period of a simple pendulum does NOT depend on the:
x: T = 2π√(L/g) contains only L and g, so the mass of the bob does not affect the period. The period changes from place to place because g changes.

q: A mass on a spring of spring constant 200 N m⁻¹ oscillates in SHM with amplitude 0.1 m. Its total energy is:
x: E = ½kx₀² = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 2 J; forgetting to square the amplitude gives ½ × 200 × 0.1 = 10 J.

q: A 0.5 kg mass on a spring of spring constant 200 N m⁻¹ oscillates in SHM with amplitude 0.1 m. Its maximum speed is:
x: ½mv₀² = ½kx₀² gives v₀ = x₀√(k/m) = 0.1 × √400 = 0.1 × 20 = 2 m s⁻¹. 20 m s⁻¹ is ω, forgetting to multiply by the amplitude.

q: A body performs SHM with amplitude x₀. At what displacement from the mean position are its kinetic and potential energies equal?
x: PE = ½kx² and total = ½kx₀²; equal shares mean ½kx² = ¼kx₀², so x = x₀/√2. Taking half the amplitude gives x₀/2, where the PE is only a quarter of the total.

q: A mass on a spring of spring constant 100 N m⁻¹ oscillates in SHM with amplitude 0.2 m. Its kinetic energy when its displacement is 0.1 m is:
x: K = ½k(x₀² − x²) = ½ × 100 × (0.04 − 0.01) = 50 × 0.03 = 1.5 J. 0.5 J is the PE at that point; 2 J is the total energy; leaving out the ½ gives 3 J.

q: The bob of a simple pendulum, mass 0.2 kg, passes its lowest point at 2 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance, how high above the lowest point does it rise at the end of its swing (g = 10 m s⁻²)?
x: KE at the bottom becomes PE at the extreme: ½mv² = mgh, so h = v²/2g = 4/20 = 0.2 m (the mass cancels). Leaving out the 2 gives 0.4 m.

q: For a mass–spring system in SHM, a graph of potential energy against displacement from the mean position is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A parabola with its maximum at the mean position
A parabola with its minimum at the mean position
x: PE = ½kx², a parabola that is zero at x = 0 and greatest at the extremes. A parabola with a maximum at the mean position describes the kinetic energy; the horizontal line is the total energy.

q: A body performs SHM with frequency f. The frequency with which its kinetic energy varies is:
x: With x = x₀ sin ωt, K = ½mω²x₀² cos²ωt = ¼mω²x₀²(1 + cos 2ωt), which varies at angular frequency 2ω, i.e. frequency 2f. Kinetic energy is greatest twice in each cycle (each pass through the mean position), so assuming f is the slip.

q: Resonance occurs in a system driven by a periodic force when:
o: The driving force is very large
The driving frequency is twice the natural frequency
The driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system
x: At resonance the driver's frequency matches the natural frequency, so energy is transferred most efficiently and the amplitude becomes largest. A large force alone does not cause resonance.

q: A simple pendulum oscillates in air and its oscillations are lightly damped. As time passes:
o: Its amplitude and its period both decrease
Its amplitude stays constant while its period increases
Its amplitude decreases while its period stays nearly the same
Its amplitude increases while its period decreases
x: Damping removes energy, so the amplitude falls gradually; for light damping the period stays almost equal to the natural period. Thinking the period shrinks with the amplitude is the common slip.

q: For a driven oscillator, the damping is increased. Compared with the lightly damped case, the graph of amplitude against driving frequency has a peak that is:
x: More damping removes more energy each cycle, so the resonant amplitude is smaller and the response is spread over a wider range of frequencies: a lower, flatter peak. Light damping gives the high, sharp peak.

q: A system is made to oscillate by a periodic driving force. Once steady oscillations are set up, the system oscillates at:
o: The frequency of the driving force
The average of its natural frequency and the driving frequency
x: In forced oscillations the system is made to follow the driver, so in the steady state it vibrates at the driving frequency; only the amplitude depends on how close this is to the natural frequency. Oscillating at the natural frequency describes free oscillations.

q: Shock absorbers are fitted to the suspension springs of a car mainly to:
o: Make the springs oscillate at resonance
Increase the natural frequency of the springs to a very high value
Store energy and return it to the car later
Damp the oscillations so the car body stops bouncing quickly
x: Shock absorbers provide damping: they turn the energy of the oscillation into heat, so the car body settles quickly after a bump instead of bouncing for a long time. They are used to prevent resonance, not to produce it.

q: A radio receiver is tuned to a particular station by:
o: Increasing the damping of its tuning circuit to a very high value
Making the receiver's circuit oscillate at twice the station's frequency
Raising the loudness until the station is heard
Adjusting the natural frequency of its tuning circuit to equal the station's frequency
x: Tuning changes the natural frequency of the receiver's circuit until it matches the frequency of the wanted station; at resonance that signal gives the largest response. Heavy damping would make the response broad, so stations would not be separated.

q: A simple pendulum 1 m long is driven by a small periodic force at a place where g = π² m s⁻². Its amplitude is largest when the driving frequency is:
x: Resonance happens at the natural frequency: T = 2π√(L/g) = 2π√(1/π²) = 2 s, so f = 1/T = 0.5 Hz. Giving the period instead of the frequency leads to 2 Hz.

q: A 1 kg mass on a spring of spring constant 100 N m⁻¹ is driven by a periodic force. Its amplitude is largest when the frequency of the driving force is:
x: Natural angular frequency ω = √(k/m) = √100 = 10 rad s⁻¹, so f = ω/2π = 10/2π = 5/π Hz (about 1.6 Hz); resonance occurs at this frequency. Giving ω as if it were the frequency gives 10 Hz.

q: Soldiers marching across a light bridge are told to break step. The reason is that their regular steps could:
o: Match a natural frequency of the bridge and build up a dangerously large amplitude
Increase the damping of the bridge too much
Lower the weight that the bridge can carry
Make the bridge oscillate at a frequency different from their steps
x: Marching in step applies a periodic force; if its frequency equals a natural frequency of the bridge, resonance makes the amplitude grow and the bridge may be damaged. Breaking step removes the regular driving frequency.
